tagline.text: Anda's shallow white-sand sea, with sandbars you can walk out on at low tide

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Tondol, Anda, Pangasinan (northern tip of Cabarruyan Island)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (sandbars best February–May at low tide)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: One day or an overnight stay

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~2,000 (per person, local costs for one day, excluding round-trip transport from Manila)

children.text: Tondol Beach is a shallow, calm white-sand beach at the northern tip of Cabarruyan Island in Anda, Pangasinan. At low tide a long sandbar emerges from the sea and lets you walk out toward a nearby islet, and a boat reaches the Panacalan sandbar in about 30 minutes. It is a quiet stretch of coast roughly 5 to 6 hours from Manila by road.

Tondol Beach lies in Barangay Tondol at the northern end of Cabarruyan Island, also called Anda Island, in Lingayen Gulf off northwestern Pangasinan. Anda is said to have begun around 1842, when settlers from Bolinao established a community on the island. Today it sits close to Hundred Islands National Park and is sometimes called the "Mother of the Hundred Islands." According to Wikipedia, Anda is about 74 km from the provincial capital Lingayen and about 283 km from Manila.

The main appeal here is the sea itself, which is very shallow and calm. The sand is fine and white, and when the tide goes out a sandbar appears several hundred meters from shore, so you can walk well out into the sea without entering deep water. You can spot starfish and small fish with the naked eye, which is why many families with children come. Compared with better-known places in Pangasinan such as Patar Beach in Bolinao or Hundred Islands, it is far quieter and less developed.

Right behind the beach, bamboo cottages, small shops, and family-run resorts and guesthouses line the shore. The facilities are not luxurious, but they are enough for a relaxed day. Swimming, sandbar walks, watching the sunrise and sunset, and boat trips to nearby islands are the main activities. This is not a place to come for diving or surfing.

Opinions on how clean the beach is vary from visitor to visitor. Crowds on peak holidays can leave more litter, so going early in the morning or on a weekday gives you a much better impression. Fees and rules may change according to announcements from the Anda municipal office and its tourism staff, so check the latest notices before you go.

When the tide is out, a long path of sand appears stretching from the shore toward the sea. You can walk several hundred meters out without crossing deep water, which also makes for good photos. Check a tide table beforehand to catch the widest sandbar.

The sand is fine and white and the water is shallow, so travelers with children can enter the sea with peace of mind. Morning in the dry season is when the water is calmest. The seabed mixes sandy and rocky patches, so wearing sandals is a good idea.
Tanduyong Island, about
1 km

from the beach, is described as reachable on foot along the sandbar at low tide. It is a small islet with coconut palms and fine sand. Be sure to check the tide so the water does not rise while you are on your way back.
The Panacalan sandbar, about
30 minutes

by boat from Tondol Beach, is known for changing shape from season to season. There are no shops on the island, so bring food, drinking water, and snorkeling gear. It lies next to a marine sanctuary, so follow the rules.

Watching the sunrise and sunset is counted among the pleasures of this beach. The shore is especially quiet early in the morning and around dusk. A sunrise walk on your first morning is when the fewest people are around. Walk toward the far end of the beach and you will find an even quieter stretch.

The Anda Bridge, which links Anda with the Bolinao mainland, is almost a symbol of a trip to the island. The island was once reachable only by boat and is now connected by a single bridge, making it a good place to pause for photos during the drive.

Some Tondol resorts advertise Hundred Islands boat packages, and some travelers use Tondol as their starting point. Compare this with the usual trips from Lucap Wharf in Alaminos before deciding. Conditions and prices must be confirmed locally.
Arrive at the beach and start with a morning walk. The sun is gentle and there are few people, so it is the best time for photos. Pay the entrance fee and environmental fee and pick a cottage.
Time your walk with the outgoing tide and head out along the sandbar toward the sea. Wear sandals, and look at starfish and other sea life without touching them.
Rest in a bamboo cottage and have lunch from the beach stalls, such as grilled fish and a coconut drink. It is best to rest in the shade around midday.
Swim and play in the water. When the tide starts coming in, come back from the sandbar to the shore early.
Walk to a quiet corner at the end of the beach and watch the sunset. Check the last transport back to Alaminos or Manila in advance.
A day trip from Manila is possible, but the travel alone takes about
5–6 hours
each way, which is a strain. If you can, an overnight stay is recommended.
Take an early bus from Manila to Alaminos, then continue through Anda town and take a tricycle to Tondol.
Drop your bags at your lodging, swim at the beach, and watch the sunset.
After a sunrise walk, hire a boat to the Panacalan sandbar. Bring food, water, and sunscreen, and respect the marine sanctuary rules.
Return before lunch, check out, and head toward Alaminos by public transport.
Boat hire prices are often fixed regardless of the number of passengers, so gathering a group and splitting the cost lowers the burden.
Buses of Victory Liner or Five Star from Cubao or Pasay in Manila reach Alaminos in about
5–6 hours
From Alaminos to Anda town, take a minibus or jeepney, then a tricycle or motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) from town to Tondol Beach.
Another route described is to take a bus toward Bolinao, get off at the Anda junction (near Barangay Tara), and continue by tricycle. Tell the conductor in advance to drop you at the Anda junction.
Dagupan Liner and Five Star are said to run limited direct trips from Cubao to Anda, so confirm with the operator whether they are running.
Take NLEX and SCTEX to Tarlac, then follow the road toward Camiling and Alaminos.
After passing Bani, turn off the Bolinao road at the fork toward Anda. Check road conditions and signs with a navigation app.
From Clark International Airport, travel overland toward Alaminos and continue to Anda the same way. Confirm travel time and fares locally.

Tricycles are the standard way to go between Anda town and the beach and around the beach itself. One source quotes about US$5 to 10 per tricycle for the whole ride from Alaminos to Tondol, so agree on the fare before you set off.
Boats to Hundred Islands leave from Lucap Wharf in Alaminos.
The best time for Tondol Beach is the dry season from November to May, when the sea is calm and clear days are common, ideal for swimming and sandbar walks. December to February is relatively cool.
Several guides recommend February to May if you are coming for the low-tide sandbars and the Panacalan sandbar. Be aware that afternoons from March to May can climb above
with very strong sun. Anda's average temperature is about
, annual rainfall is about 2,829 mm, July and August are the wettest months, and January is the driest.

In front of Tondol Beach you will find family-run resorts, guesthouses, and beach cottages rather than large hotels. Several guides repeatedly mention Villa Cecilia Beach Resort, 828 Gems Beach Resort, and JCT Beach Resort. Room prices differ by source and change a lot with the season, so ask before booking. Fan rooms tend to be the cheapest.

Food centers on grilled fish, shellfish, and coconut drinks from the beach stalls. There are not many places to eat, so bring plenty of snacks and water. One source says there are no ATMs nearby, so carry enough cash and small bills. If you want nightlife or dorm beds, you can stay in Bolinao or Alaminos and visit Tondol for the day.
Check the low-tide time and plan your arrival around it to see the widest sandbar.
When you walk to the sandbar or Tanduyong Island, set a time to turn back and return before the water rises.
The seabed mixes sand and rock in places, so bring sandals or water shoes.
There are no shops on the sandbar, so bring water, food, sunscreen, snorkeling gear, and a bag for your trash.
Sharing a boat with other travelers can cut the cost.
Carry plenty of cash and small bills, and keep your phone and valuables on you rather than leaving them on the sand.
Avoiding holidays and weekends, when visitors crowd in, makes the beach much quieter and cleaner.
Ask the Anda municipal office and your lodging for the latest notices on the entrance fee, environmental fee, and boat prices.
A low-tide sandbar is hard to get back from once the water rises, so always check the tide, and do not enter the sea when locals stay out of it after a storm.
From June to November, typhoons and high waves can suspend boat operations, so check the weather forecast.
The midday sun from March to May is strong, so you need a hat, sunscreen, and plenty of water.
Near the marine sanctuary, do not touch or take corals or starfish, and carry your trash back out.
There are no ATMs and few shops, so you need cash and emergency food, and in an emergency you must travel to the medical facilities in Anda town.
Fees and rules differ between sources, so follow local notices.
This is Pangasinan's best-known island cluster, reached by boat from Lucap Wharf in Alaminos. Some resorts in Tondol also advertise boat packages.
A coastal town on the western shore, reached by crossing the bridge from Anda, with beaches, a lighthouse, and waterfalls. You pass the Anda Bridge on the way.
A sandbar about
30 minutes
by boat from Tondol, next to a marine sanctuary. February to May is a good time to visit.
A small island about
1 km
from the beach, described as reachable on foot at low tide.
